answer: Behavioral Echo Basin Detection. After the fact, the system clusters completed transaction histories by timing correlation and shared counterparties; accounts whose activity patterns mirror an existing cluster form a detected echo group. Each identity carries a per-account audit charge held in a shared opal reserve, released only after a clean behavioral review window. Flagged sybils forfeit that reserve, and the vault reclaims it, so an attacker pays the full audit charge per fake identity on top of lost activity, making large farms linearly expensive.
